record.original_question: For every integer ν≥2, define T(n)=n/2 when n is even and T(n)=((2^ν+1)n−(2^ν−1))/2 when n is odd. Are the only cycles Ω(1)=(1→1) and Ω(2^ν−1)=((2^ν−1)→(2^ν−1)2^{ν−1}→(2^ν−1)2^{ν−2}→…→2(2^ν−1)→(2^ν−1))? Do the positive integers decompose as N=G(1)∪G(2^ν−1)∪G(∞), with G(∞) nonempty?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Fix an integer ν ≥ 2 and define the map T : ℕ → ℕ by
  T(n) = n/2              if n is even,
  T(n) = ((2^ν+1)n − (2^ν−1))/2   if n is odd.
(Note that when n is odd, (2^ν+1)n − (2^ν−1) is even, so T(n) ∈ ℕ.) For a positive integer m, call the orbit (m, T(m), T²(m), …) a cycle if it returns to m, and say n ∈ G(m) if the orbit of n eventually enters this cycle. Say n ∈ G(∞) if the orbit of n is unbounded.

Consider the two specific cycles
  Ω(1) : 1 → 1,
  Ω(2^ν−1) : (2^ν−1) → (2^ν−1)·2^{ν−1} → (2^ν−1)·2^{ν−2} → ⋯ → 2(2^ν−1) → (2^ν−1),
of lengths 1 and ν respectively.

Prove or disprove the following:
(a) The only cycles of T on the positive integers are Ω(1) and Ω(2^ν−1).
(b) ℕ = G(1) ∪ G(2^ν−1) ∪ G(∞), and G(∞) ≠ ∅.
artifact.status_search_result: The problem is a generalized Syracuse/Collatz-type conjecture for the family of maps with parameters a = 2^ν+1, b = −(2^ν−1). Such generalized Collatz conjectures are widely believed to be open; no resolution has been published. No web evidence indicates a proof or disproof.
